Reappraisal of ‘Urban Political Structure and Inequality: Political Economy Lessons from Early Modern German Cities’ (Schaff, 2024)

MY457 | WT 2026

Author

62628

Published

July 31, 2026

Introduction

This reappraisal evaluates Schaff (2024), who asks whether closed (oligarchic) political institutions caused higher wealth inequality in preindustrial Germany. The paper combines a panel of 33 cities (1500–1800) with a micro-level panel of taxpayer-year observations from Nördlingen (1579–1700), using the second to identify mechanisms behind the first. Identification at the individual level rests on a staggered, absorbing difference-in-differences design estimated with the heterogeneity-robust estimators of de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) and de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2024) (henceforth DCDH), supplemented by a triple-difference that exploits the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648) as a plausibly exogenous shock to magistrates’ opportunities for self-enrichment.

The paper’s methodological contribution is non-trivial. The closest prior work on returns to public office (Eggers and Hainmueller 2009) relies on TWFE, which under staggered timing produces biased estimates of the ATT (Goodman-Bacon 2021). Schaff (2024) anticipates this by adopting the DCDH estimator throughout, reporting TWFE counterparts in his Online Appendix 5. This leaves unaddressed a complementary issue — sensitivity to parallel-trends violations (Rambachan and Roth 2023) — which motivates Section 5.

Nördlingen’s Hasenräte constitution1 selected magistrates by co-optation for life, producing the clean staggered design exploited by the paper. I reproduce the main individual- and city-level results, document where the estimates depart from the published ones and why, and then probe the parallel-trends concern using the sensitivity framework of Rambachan and Roth (2023), which the paper does not implement.

Research Design

Research Question

The empirical question is: what is the causal effect of holding political office on personal wealth and the wealth distribution, in a closed (oligarchic) political system?

Three sub-questions follow: (i) does the macro-level association between closed structures and wealth concentration align with the micro-level office effect? (ii) was the effect amplified during the Thirty Years’ War? (iii) which mechanism — compensation, business, patronage, or embezzlement — explains the enrichment?

Data

The author combines two hand-digitised datasets (construction details in his Online Appendix 1). The city-level dataset covers 33 German cities at 25-year intervals between 1500 and 1800. Top wealth shares (10%, 5%, 1%) come from Schaff (2022); the indicator for participatory council elections is coded from Keyser and Stoob (1939). Five additional controls capture conflict intensity, log population, epidemic incidence, Protestant Reformation introduction, and log distance to the nearest university.

The individual-level dataset contains 21,579 observations of 4,490 taxpayers across 22 unequally-spaced periods between 1579 and 1700 — irregular periodicity reflecting the historical schedule of Nördlingen’s Steuerregister. Of these, 70 taxpayers eventually became magistrates. Variables include wealth outcomes (log wealth, percentile, top-5% indicator), treatments (council-membership, mayor, and city-clerk indicators), demographic controls, and mechanism variables (council-inheritance indicator, Thirty Years’ War period indicator). The unit of analysis is the city-year (city panel) and the taxpayer-year (individual panel).

Identification Strategy

Estimands and Specifications

The city-level analysis estimates a TWFE regression on the 33-city dataset:

\[ I_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \pi_t + \beta\,\text{Election}_{i,t} + \gamma' X_{i,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \tag{1}\]

where \(I_{i,t}\) is a top wealth share in city \(i\) at year \(t\), \(\alpha_i\) and \(\pi_t\) are city and year fixed effects, \(\text{Election}_{i,t}\) is a dummy for participatory elections, and \(X_{i,t}\) contains the five controls listed in Section 2.2. Standard errors are clustered at the city level. The treatment is non-absorbing — cities switch in and out of electoral systems — TWFE targets a weighted average of \(2\times 2\) comparisons with potentially negative weights (Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020), the author therefore treats these as conditional correlations rather than causal estimates; I discuss this further in Section 4.

The individual-level analysis is a staggered DiD on the Nördlingen panel, comparing wealth trajectories of taxpayers who eventually enter the council with those who never do:

\[ W_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \pi_t + \beta\,(\text{Council}_i \times \text{Post}_{i,t}) + \gamma' X_{i,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \tag{2}\]

where \(W_{i,t}\) is a wealth outcome (log wealth, wealth percentile, or top-5% indicator) measured at intervals of three to six years between 1585 and 1700, \(\text{Council}_i = 1\) if individual \(i\) ever joins the council, \(\text{Post}_{i,t} = 1\) for periods at or after \(i\) joins the council, and \(X_{i,t}\) is a vector of time-varying covariates specified in three nested versions detailed below. The coefficient \(\beta\) captures the ATT of council membership.2

For each outcome, three nested versions of Equation 2 are estimated — corresponding to the three columns of Schaff’s Table 3 — varying the content of \(X_{i,t}\): (i) Only FE: \(X_{i,t} = \emptyset\); (ii) Baseline: \(X_{i,t} = (\text{ntaxpayments}, \text{ntaxpayments}^2)\), a life-cycle proxy; (iii) Baseline + Controls: further adds the 61 occupational dummies and a gender indicator.

The flexible (event-study) variant estimates a separate coefficient for each event-time period:

\[ W_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \pi_t + \sum_{k=-2}^{7} \beta_k\,(\text{Council}_i \times \mathbf{1}\{\text{PeriodsToCouncil}_{i,t} = k\}) + \gamma' X_{i,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \tag{3}\]

where \(k\) indexes event time relative to council entry, \(k=-1\) is the omitted reference, and the \(\beta_k\) for \(k < 0\) are placebo coefficients.3

The triple-difference design for Table 5 exploits the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1646) as a quasi-exogenous shock:

\[ W_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \pi_t + \beta_1(\text{Council}_i \times \text{Post}_{i,t} \times \text{30YearsWar}_t) + \beta_2(\text{Council}_i \times \text{Post}_{i,t}) + \gamma' X_{i,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \tag{4}\]

\(\beta_1\) captures the additional war-period effect on top of the baseline office effect \(\beta_2\). All individual-level specifications are estimated with the de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) estimator on the relevant sample (full panel for Equation 2 and Equation 3; 1603–1646 for Equation 4), with 100-replication block-bootstrap standard errors clustered at the household level.

Validating the Assumptions

Causal identification rests on three assumptions.

1. Conditional parallel trends. In the absence of treatment, the change in wealth between any two periods would have been the same, on average, for future magistrates as for non-magistrates, conditional on the time-varying covariates \(X_{i,t}\).

2. No anticipation. Future magistrates do not adjust their wealth-accumulation behaviour before entering the council. Formally, if \(G_i\) denotes the period \(i\) enters the council and \(W^*_{i,t}(0)\) the potential wealth under control of an anticipator, the assumption requires \(E[W_{i,t}(0) \mid G_i = g] = E[W^*_{i,t}(0) \mid G_i = g]\) for all \(t < g\).

3. SUTVA. No-interference requires that magistrate enrichment does not mechanically affect non-magistrates’ wealth — non-trivial in Nördlingen, where 15 magistrates exercised lifetime control over a closed municipal budget, making the channels of enrichment (compensation, patronage, embezzlement) zero-sum with respect to the taxpayer base. Treatment consistency requires “entering the council” to be homogeneous, but tenure varies from years to decades and the role differs in peacetime vs. wartime. SUTVA is not discussed by the author; I return to it in Section 4.

Main Results Replication

The replication is implemented in R, translating the Stata .do file from Schaff (2024)’s replication package. The principal command (did_multiplegt in Stata) maps to DIDmultiplegtDYN::did_multiplegt_dyn() in R — a related but not identical implementation, which produces small numerical discrepancies that I document where they arise. All heavy estimations are pre-computed in replication.R and loaded into this document from output/*.rds; see README.md for instructions.4

Empirical Setup

Pre-treatment Characteristics of Future Magistrates (Table 1)

Table 1 compares the pre-office characteristics of future magistrates with those of the rest of the taxpaying population.

Future magistrates were on average 2.5 log points wealthier (~12 times richer in levels) and scored 42 percentile points higher in the wealth distribution before entering office. They were significantly more likely to be city clerks, merchants, or in writing occupations, and significantly less likely to be women or wool weavers. This selection on observables is what motivates the author’s DiD strategy: a naive post-treatment comparison would conflate the office effect with magistrates’ pre-existing wealth advantage. DiD requires equality of trends, not balance in levels (Section 2.3); Table 1 here characterises the treatment group and quantifies the magnitude of self-selection — a concern revisited in Section 4.

City-Level Association: cities with vs. without elections (Table 2)

Table 2 reports the TWFE panel regression of Equation 1: a city-level association between political openness and wealth concentration across 33 cities.

Cities with participatory council elections had top wealth shares 4–6 percentage points lower than cities without, with the largest absolute effect on the top 5% share. Point estimates, standard errors, and within-R² values replicate the published Table 2 to the third decimal across all six columns. As discussed in Section 2.3, these are conditional correlations rather than causal effects given non-absorbing treatment, and serve only as motivation for the individual-level analysis that follows.

Main causal estimate: the office effect

The main causal claim is identified at the individual level, where the treatment — entry into the city council — is staggered and absorbing. Table 3 reports the ATT under the de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) estimator, and Figure 1 traces its dynamic profile to probe the parallel-trends assumption.

Individual-Level DiD (Table 3)

Table 3 reports the main DiD estimates of the effect of council membership on personal wealth.

The replication reproduces the direction, significance, and broad magnitude of the published estimates. Council membership is associated with substantial wealth gains: an ATT of ~0.40 log points (Baseline) on log wealth, 2–3 percentile points on wealth rank, and 9–10 percentage points on top-5% membership. Mayors experience additional wealth gains beyond the ordinary council effect, with my Mayor estimates (rows 8–9) reproducing the published ATTs of 0.302 and 0.339 to the third decimal.

The Council estimates (rows 1–5) are systematically smaller than the published values — the ln-wealth Baseline ATT is 0.396 (SE 0.108) here versus 0.526 (SE 0.162) in Schaff (2024) — and my analysis sample is 16,110 versus 16,315 observations (a 1.3% gap). The discrepancy concentrates in outcomes with more missing data (wealthpercentile shows the largest gap, top5percent essentially none) and disappears in the Mayor specifications, which use a balanced sub-sample (9,727 observations identical to the paper). The pattern suggests the divergence reflects how did_multiplegt (Stata) and did_multiplegt_dyn (R) handle missing observations in unbalanced panels rather than an algorithmic difference. The substantive conclusions — direction, significance, relative magnitudes — replicate cleanly.

Dynamics and Pre-trends

Figure 1 traces the dynamic effects of council membership across event time, replicating the Baseline panels of Figure 3 of Schaff (2024).5

In the ln-wealth panel (A.I), all three pre-treatment coefficients are negative and statistically significant (\(\hat\beta_{-4} \approx -0.51\); \(\hat\beta_{-3} \approx -0.48\); \(\hat\beta_{-2} \approx -0.30\)), comparable in absolute magnitude to the post-treatment ATT. The author acknowledges only the closest placebo (\(k=-2\)) and attributes it to magistrates’ prior service on the city court (p. 537), but Figure 3 of the paper trims to two placebos via trimlead(2); retaining the third reveals a monotonic pre-trend deeper than the paper documents. Panels B.I and C.I show non-zero placebos in the same direction with wider confidence intervals — including a significant \(k=-4\) in C.I. The pre-trend is not confined to ln-wealth: future magistrates were moving differentially across multiple wealth dimensions before entry, with the strongest signal in absolute wealth. Parallel trends — the core assumption of the DCDH estimator (Section 2.3) — appears violated in ln-wealth and questionable in positional outcomes. The Rambachan and Roth (2023) sensitivity exercise in Section 5 quantifies how large the post-treatment violation would have to be to overturn the conclusion.

Mechanism Tests (Table 4 and Figure 4)

The paper discriminates among four candidate channels of magistrate enrichment: dynastic inheritance, business opportunities, patronage, and formal compensation.

Inheritance (rows 1–2) is statistically indistinguishable from zero, ruling out dynastic transmission. The merchant interaction (rows 5–6) is also insignificant, weakening the business-opportunities hypothesis. The city-clerk effect (rows 7–8) is large, positive, and significant: clerks experienced wealth gains comparable to magistrates themselves despite never sitting on the council — evidence the author reads as rent-sharing (patronage).6

Figure 2 confirms the clerk effect accumulates gradually post-entry with no significant pre-trend — a cleaner identification profile than Figure 1 since the prior-court-service concern does not extend to clerks.

Robustness: The Thirty Years’ War Shock

The Thirty Years’ War (1618–1646) provides a shock to magistrates’ rent-extraction opportunities arguably unrelated to their individual characteristics. Table 5 reports the triple-difference ATT on the restricted sample 1603–1646; Figure 3 traces its dynamic profile; Figure 4 examines the parallel patronage channel through city clerks.

Wealth gains from council membership were amplified substantially during the war: the Baseline specification (row 2) yields an additional 0.42 log points on top of the peace-time office effect, rising to 0.57 with controls (row 3). Replication is closer than for Table 3 — point estimates differ from the published values by 0.02–0.20 across all seven rows, and the sample (3,339 vs 3,354) differs by only 0.4%, reflecting the more balanced 1603–1646 window. The “exogeneity” of the war as a shock to enrichment is, however, partial: it opened multiple channels simultaneously (emergency taxation, requisitioning, exemptions, credit access), and the triple-difference cannot disentangle them. What is identified is the differential wealth trajectory of officeholders during a period of mechanically expanded discretion, not specifically “enrichment from office” — a bundled-treatment concern discussed further in Section 4.

Post-treatment effects accumulate gradually and peak around four periods post-onset, but the pre-treatment placebos in Panel A.I are not uniformly null: \(\hat\beta_{-4} \approx -0.70\) with CI \([-1.1, -0.4]\) is statistically significant. The published Figure 5 trims visually to \(k=-3,-2\) via trimlead(2); retaining the third placebo shows that the parallel-trends assumption of the triple-difference is itself questionable in the more distant pre-period.

Figure 4 traces the same exercise for clerks: post-treatment effects rise substantially during the war (peak at \(k=3\), coef ≈ 2.2), mirroring Figure 3 and supporting the patronage interpretation. The clerk pre-trend is non-trivial at \(k=-3\) (coef ≈ −0.25) though noisier, in line with the smaller treated group.

Critical Reappraisal

The paper’s three central findings reproduce: the city-level association (Table 2), the individual-level office effect (Table 3), and its wartime amplification (Table 5). The patronage channel (Table 4, Figure 2) emerges as the best-supported mechanism. One pattern, however, emerges from this reappraisal that the published paper does not document. In each of the three event-studies (Figure 1, Figure 3, Figure 4), Schaff (2024) calls did_multiplegt with placebo(3) dynamic(5) but the published figures display only \(k=-3,-2\) via trimlead(2). Retaining the third placebo reveals a consistent pattern of negative, statistically significant pre-treatment coefficients in the most distant pre-period — for the council main result (\(\hat\beta_{-4} \approx -0.51\)), the war × council interaction (\(\hat\beta_{-4} \approx -0.70\)), and the clerk dynamics (\(\hat\beta_{-4} \approx -0.25\)). The pre-trend the author acknowledges only at \(k=-2\) (p. 537) is therefore deeper and more systematic than the published analysis suggests, motivating the formal sensitivity exercise in Section 5.

Research Design

Pre-trends and No-Anticipation. The placebos in Panel A.I of Figure 1 are comparable in absolute magnitude to the post-treatment ATT (\(\hat\beta_0 \approx 0.40\)). The author attributes them to magistrates’ prior court service, but pre-trend tests have low power and a significant placebo does not by itself signal the direction of post-treatment bias (Rambachan and Roth 2023). The pattern appears most clearly in level outcomes (ln-wealth) and weaker in positional outcomes (percentile, top 5%) — consistent with the prior-court-service interpretation but not exclusive of differential life-cycle accumulation.

SUTVA. No-interference is plausibly violated through two opposing channels: if magistrate enrichment came at the expense of the city treasury, controls were paying for treated gains (upward bias); if magistrates engaged in rent-sharing with allies, controls were partially “treated” by spillover (downward bias). The clerk effect in Table 4 and Figure 4 is direct evidence the second channel operates. Consistency is also strained: council service is heterogeneous in duration (years to decades), role, and historical period (peace vs. war), yet treated identically by the estimator. SUTVA is not discussed in the paper.

Measurement

The wealth coding \(\ln(\text{wealth} + 0.1)\) preserves zero-wealth observations but the choice of \(c = 0.1\) is consequential: changing it shifts the level of every coefficient and, because parallel trends is not invariant to nonlinear transformations of the outcome, also shifts the pre-trend. The author shows the conclusions are stable across alternative codings (Online Appendix 5) but does not test whether the pre-trend itself is sensitive to \(c\) — leaving open whether the documented violation is a feature of the underlying data or an artifact of the chosen transformation.

Estimation

City-level TWFE with non-absorbing treatment. Equation 1 cannot be read causally: the TWFE coefficient is a weighted average of \(2\times 2\) comparisons with potentially negative weights (Goodman-Bacon 2021), and none of the recent heterogeneity-robust alternatives (Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021; Sun and Abraham 2021; Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess 2024; de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2024) fully accommodate non-absorbing treatment. The paper integrates the city-level results into the causal narrative; a more cautious framing would treat them as motivating correlations.

Single-estimator analysis. The individual-level analysis relies on the DCDH estimator. The lecture material highlights Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) as the canonical “flexible matching and re-weighting” alternative; the two estimators belong to the same family and would not be expected to yield qualitatively different ATTs.7 The author’s Online Appendix 5 compares DCDH against conventional TWFE; what is not assessed is sensitivity to assumed parallel trends — the gap addressed in Section 5.

Reproducibility across software platforms. Four technical obstacles complicate full reproduction in R: (i) the Stata command used by the author is superseded by its developers (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2024); (ii) the R and Stata implementations differ in their handling of missing observations, producing systematic sample-size gaps (e.g., 16,110 vs 16,315 in Table 3); (iii) the R backend (polars) accumulates memory when running high-dimensional control specifications, causing “+ Controls” panels of Figure 1 to fail even on 32+ GB machines; (iv) alternative installation paths (DIDmultiplegt CRAN wrapper, did_multiplegt_old mode, GitHub development version) each fail in this setting for distinct reasons documented in the code appendix. The substantive implication is that the “+ Controls” specifications cannot in practice be verified by researchers without Stata access — a concern about accessibility and verifiability of empirical results, distinct from the validity of the headline findings.

Contribution

The event-study evidence in Figure 1 documents pre-treatment placebos that are negative and statistically significant across all three pre-periods. This raises a question the paper does not formally address: how large would the parallel-trends violation have to be to overturn the conclusion that council membership increased wealth?

Rambachan and Roth (2023) propose bounding the bias of the DiD estimator under restricted classes of parallel-trends violations and producing “robust” confidence intervals valid under those restrictions. The relative magnitudes variant constrains the post-treatment differential trend to be at most \(\bar M\) times the maximum observed pre-treatment violation; the breakdown \(\bar M\) is the largest value at which the robust CI still excludes zero. Higher breakdown values indicate stronger robustness.8

Figure 5 plots the robust CIs across values of \(\bar M\). The conventional (blue) interval excludes zero with a comfortable margin (\([0.08, 0.50]\)). The robust (red) intervals tell a more cautious story: the breakdown is reached between \(\bar M = 0\) and \(\bar M = 0.25\) — as soon as the post-treatment violation is allowed to be one-quarter as large as the worst pre-period violation, the robust 95% CI begins to include zero.

The breakdown value is low — substantially lower than what would license treating the parallel-trends assumption as plausibly innocuous. The office effect on ln-wealth is robust to a zero violation but fragile under any positive violation of comparable magnitude to the pre-period pattern. Schaff (2024) argues that the pre-trend reflects court service rather than anticipation (p. 537), in which case the post-treatment violation should be small (court service ends when council service begins). The sensitivity analysis cannot adjudicate that historical interpretation, but it makes the dependence of the conclusion on the interpretation quantitative and explicit: the headline finding survives only if the post-treatment differential trend is essentially zero, an assertion the data alone cannot test.9

The sensitivity exercise does not overturn the paper’s findings: post-treatment estimates remain large and statistically significant under conventional inference. What it establishes is that the formal identification rests on stronger assumptions than the paper acknowledges, and that the parallel-trends violation flagged but minimised in the original analysis is, by formal robustness criteria, not minor.

# Paths (reproducible across machines via here::here())
data_dir <- here::here("data")
out_dir  <- here::here("output")

# Reproducibility
set.seed(123456789)

# Consistent ggplot theme across all event-study figures
theme_schaff <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.3),
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "plain", size = 11),
    axis.title       = element_text(size = 10)
  )
# =============================================================================
# Load data
# =============================================================================

df_noe <- read_dta(file.path(data_dir, "Noerdlingen_panel_replication_JEH.dta"))
df_city <- read_dta(file.path(data_dir, "City_panel_replication_JEH.dta"))

# Validation: catch silent changes in the underlying datasets
stopifnot(
  nrow(df_noe)  == 21579,
  nrow(df_city) > 0,
  "councilmemberterm" %in% names(df_noe),
  "electionparticipation" %in% names(df_city)

# Derived variables

# Time-invariant indicator: 1 if individual ever joins the council
df_noe <- df_noe %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  mutate(councilmember_tinvar = as.integer(
    any(councilmemberterm == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
  )) %>%
  ungroup()

# Subset used in the Thirty Years' War triple-difference (Table 5, Figs 5-6)
df_30yw <- df_noe %>% filter(units_30yw == 1, year >= 1603, year <= 1646)

# Occupational dummies used as controls
occ_vars <- grep("^occupation_", names(df_noe), value = TRUE)

# Counts used in inline references throughout the document
n_magistrates <- length(unique(df_noe$ID[df_noe$councilmember_tinvar == 1]))
# =============================================================================
# Helper functions used throughout the document
# =============================================================================

# Extract ATT (period 1) from a did_multiplegt_dyn result, returning a tibble row
extract_dcdh_summary <- function(res, label_y, label_spec) {
  eff <- res$results$Effects
  tibble(
    Outcome       = label_y,
    Specification = label_spec,
    ATT           = round(eff[1, "Estimate"], 3),
    SE            = round(eff[1, "SE"],       3),
    Up_95_CI      = round(eff[1, "UB CI"],    3),
    Lo_95_CI      = round(eff[1, "LB CI"],    3),
    N             = eff[1, "N"]
  )
}

# Plot a single event-study panel in the paper's style.
# Placebos returned by did_multiplegt_dyn are indexed 1..K with Placebo_1 being
# the period immediately before the omitted reference k=-1
plot_event_dcdh <- function(res, title = "", y_label = "Treatment effect") {
  pl <- as.data.frame(res$results$Placebos)
  pl$period <- -(seq_len(nrow(pl)) + 1)   

  ef <- as.data.frame(res$results$Effects)
  ef$period <- seq_len(nrow(ef)) - 1       

  names(pl)[names(pl) == "Estimate"] <- "est"
  names(ef)[names(ef) == "Estimate"] <- "est"
  names(pl)[names(pl) == "LB CI"]    <- "lb"
  names(ef)[names(ef) == "LB CI"]    <- "lb"
  names(pl)[names(pl) == "UB CI"]    <- "ub"
  names(ef)[names(ef) == "UB CI"]    <- "ub"

  df_plot <- bind_rows(
    pl %>% select(period, est, lb, ub),
    ef %>% select(period, est, lb, ub)
  )

  ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = period, y = est)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "red",
               linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), width = 0.1, color = "navy") +
    geom_point(color = "navy", size = 2) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Periods since the event", y = y_label) +
    theme_schaff
}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Note on the pre-Council sample filter:
# The original Stata code defines the pre-Council sample using a set of
# periodstocouncil_pX dummies that are referenced but not included in the
# replication .dta file distributed via ICPSR. I approximate the filter
# using councilmemberterm == 0, which yields the same direction and
# magnitude for all coefficients reported below but admits a slightly larger
# sample for future magistrates in their pre-entry years.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

df_pre <- df_noe %>% filter(councilmemberterm == 0)

vars_balance <- c("logwealth", "wealthpercentile", "top5percent",
                  "ntaxpayments", "womentaxpayer", "cityadmin_f",
                  "occupation_500", "occupation_640",
                  "occupation_900", "occupation_100")

get_balance_row <- function(var) {
  fml <- as.formula(paste(var, "~ councilmember_tinvar"))
  m   <- lm(fml, data = df_pre)
  tibble(
    variable = var,
    diff     = coef(m)["councilmember_tinvar"],
    se       = sqrt(vcov(m)["councilmember_tinvar", "councilmember_tinvar"]),
    p_value  = summary(m)$coefficients["councilmember_tinvar", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    mean_all = mean(df_pre[[var]], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

tab1 <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_balance, get_balance_row)

labels_tab1 <- c(
  logwealth        = "Wealth (Log) pre council",
  wealthpercentile = "Wealth percentile pre council",
  top5percent      = "Top 5 percent pre council",
  ntaxpayments     = "Nr. of tax payments pre council",
  womentaxpayer    = "Share of women pre council",
  cityadmin_f      = "City clerk pre council",
  occupation_500   = "Merchant pre council",
  occupation_640   = "Writing occupation pre council",
  occupation_900   = "Without occupation (Wealth > 1 fl.) pre council",
  occupation_100   = "Wool weaver pre council"
)

tab1 %>%
  mutate(
    stars = case_when(
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.10 ~ "*",
      TRUE           ~ ""
    ),
    diff_se = paste0(formatC(diff, digits = 2, format = "f"), stars,
                     " (", formatC(se, digits = 2, format = "f"), ")"),
    mean_all = formatC(mean_all, digits = 2, format = "f"),
    variable_label = labels_tab1[variable]
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    Variable                  = variable_label,
    `Diff (treat - rest)`     = diff_se,
    `Mean (all pre-Council)`  = mean_all
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = Variable) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = -Variable) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(12),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
    column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(2)
  )
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Manual within-FE estimator matching Stata `xtreg, fe vce(cluster)` exactly.
# Demeans y and X by IDlocality, includes yearineq25 dummies in X, computes
# cluster-robust SEs with Stata's small-sample correction, and reports the
# within-R² as 1 - SSR/SST_demeaned (Stata convention). fixest::feols does not
# reproduce Stata's within-R² out of the box, so the estimator is rewritten
# from scratch to match the published Table 2 exactly.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_city_fe <- function(data, y, controls = character()) {
  vars <- c(y, "electionparticipation", controls, "yearineq25", "IDlocality")
  d <- data[, vars] |> na.omit()
  d$yearineq25 <- factor(d$yearineq25)

  rhs <- c("electionparticipation", controls, "yearineq25")
  X <- model.matrix(
    as.formula(paste("~", paste(rhs, collapse = " + "))),
    data = d
  )
  X <- X[, colnames(X) != "(Intercept)", drop = FALSE]

  id    <- d$IDlocality
  y_raw <- as.numeric(d[[y]])

  # Demean by city FE
  y_dm <- y_raw - ave(y_raw, id, FUN = mean)
  X_dm <- apply(X, 2, function(z) z - ave(z, id, FUN = mean))
  X_dm <- as.matrix(X_dm)

  fit  <- lm.fit(x = X_dm, y = y_dm)
  beta <- coef(fit)
  u    <- residuals(fit)

  # Cluster-robust variance with Stata's small-sample correction
  XtX_inv <- solve(crossprod(X_dm))
  meat    <- matrix(0, ncol(X_dm), ncol(X_dm))
  for (g in unique(id)) {
    idx <- id == g
    xu  <- crossprod(X_dm[idx, , drop = FALSE], u[idx])
    meat <- meat + xu %*% t(xu)
  }

  G <- length(unique(id))
  N <- nrow(d)
  K <- ncol(X_dm) + 1                                # Stata counts the constant
  stata_correction <- (G / (G - 1)) * ((N - 1) / (N - K))
  V  <- stata_correction * XtX_inv %*% meat %*% XtX_inv
  se <- sqrt(diag(V))

  tibble(
    outcome   = y,
    controls  = length(controls) > 0,
    beta      = beta["electionparticipation"],
    se        = se["electionparticipation"],
    N         = N,
    cities    = G,
    within_r2 = 1 - sum(u^2) / sum(y_dm^2),
    mean_y    = mean(y_raw)
  )
}

# Run the six regressions reported in the paper's Table 2
controls_city <- c("conflict25", "logpopulation", "epidemic",
                   "reformationintro", "loguniversitydist")

t2 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  run_city_fe(df_city, "D10"),
  run_city_fe(df_city, "D10",  controls_city),
  run_city_fe(df_city, "Top5"),
  run_city_fe(df_city, "Top5", controls_city),
  run_city_fe(df_city, "Top1"),
  run_city_fe(df_city, "Top1", controls_city)
)

# Significance stars based on cluster-robust t-stats with Stata's df = G - 1
t2 <- t2 %>%
  mutate(
    t_stat   = beta / se,
    p_val    = 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = cities - 1),
    stars    = case_when(
      p_val < 0.01 ~ "***",
      p_val < 0.05 ~ "**",
      p_val < 0.10 ~ "*",
      TRUE         ~ ""
    ),
    coef_fmt = sprintf("%.3f%s", beta, stars),
    se_fmt   = sprintf("(%.3f)", se)
  )

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The Rambachan-Roth (2023) sensitivity procedure  requires a TWFE event-study 
# with a non-diagonal vcov. I estimate the same event-study as 
# Figure 3 Panel A.I but with two-way FE(the specification reported by 
# Schaff in Online Appendix Table A5.1) so the residuals carry the correlations 
# across event-times that did_multiplegt_dyn discards. 
# The point estimates differ slightly from the DCDH baseline; what
# matters here is the sensitivity profile, not the level of the ATT.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Build event-time variable: k = periodID - first_council_period
# Cap at [-4, +4] to match Figure 3's range; bin extremes.
df_es <- df_noe %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  mutate(
    first_council = if (any(councilmemberterm == 1, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      min(periodID[councilmemberterm == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    }
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    event_time   = ifelse(is.na(first_council), NA_real_,
                          periodID - first_council),
    # Bin endpoints to avoid extreme event-times with few observations
    event_time_b = case_when(
      is.na(event_time)     ~ -1L,            # never-treated = reference
      event_time <= -4       ~ -4L,
      event_time >=  4       ~  4L,
      TRUE                   ~ as.integer(event_time)
    ),
    # k = -1 is the omitted reference; never-treated also pooled with k=-1
    event_time_b = factor(event_time_b, levels = c(-1, -4, -3, -2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4))
  )

# Estimate TWFE event-study
es_twfe <- feols(
  logwealth ~ event_time_b + ntaxpayments + I(ntaxpayments^2) |
    ID + periodID,
  data    = df_es,
  cluster = ~ ID
)

# Extract betahat and sigma in the order HonestDiD expects:
# pre-periods first (most distant to closest), then post-periods (k=0 to k=4)
event_names <- c("event_time_b-4", "event_time_b-3", "event_time_b-2",
                 "event_time_b0",  "event_time_b1",  "event_time_b2",
                 "event_time_b3",  "event_time_b4")

betahat <- coef(es_twfe)[event_names]
sigma   <- vcov(es_twfe)[event_names, event_names]

# Sanity check: vcov has non-trivial off-diagonal elements
off_diag <- sigma[lower.tri(sigma)]
stopifnot(max(abs(off_diag)) > 0)

# Apply Rambachan-Roth sensitivity with relative-magnitudes restriction
sens_log <- HonestDiD::createSensitivityResults_relativeMagnitudes(
  betahat        = betahat,
  sigma          = sigma,
  numPrePeriods  = 3,
  numPostPeriods = 5,
  Mbarvec        = seq(0, 2, by = 0.25)
)

# Original (non-robust) CI for benchmark
orig_ci <- HonestDiD::constructOriginalCS(
  betahat        = betahat,
  sigma          = sigma,
  numPrePeriods  = 3,
  numPostPeriods = 5
)

# Plot
HonestDiD::createSensitivityPlot_relativeMagnitudes(
  robustResults   = sens_log,
  originalResults = orig_ci
) +
  labs(
    x = expression(bar(M)),
    y = "95% CI on ATT at k=0 (ln-wealth)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_schaff +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

References

Borusyak, Kirill, Xavier Jaravel, and Jann Spiess. 2024. “Revisiting Event-Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation.” Review of Economic Studies.
Callaway, Brantly, and Pedro H. C. Sant’Anna. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 200–230.
de Chaisemartin, Clément, and Xavier D’Haultfœuille. 2020. “Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” American Economic Review 110 (9): 2964–96.
———. 2024. “Difference-in-Differences Estimators of Intertemporal Treatment Effects.” Review of Economics and Statistics.
Eggers, Andrew C., and Jens Hainmueller. 2009. “MPs for Sale? Returns to Office in Postwar British Politics.” American Political Science Review 103 (4): 513–33.
Goodman-Bacon, Andrew. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 254–77.
Keyser, Erich, and Heinz Stoob, eds. 1939. Deutsches Städtebuch: Handbuch Städtischer Geschichte. Stuttgart: W. Kohlhammer Verlag.
Rambachan, Ashesh, and Jonathan Roth. 2023. “A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends.” Review of Economic Studies 90 (5): 2555–91.
Schaff, Felix. 2022. “Urban Wealth Inequality in Preindustrial Germany.” European Review of Economic History.
———. 2024. “Urban Political Structure and Inequality: Political Economy Lessons from Early Modern German Cities.” The Journal of Economic History 84 (2): 517–53. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022050724000135.
Sun, Liyang, and Sarah Abraham. 2021. “Estimating Dynamic Treatment Effects in Event Studies with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 175–99.

Footnotes

  1. Charles V imposed the constitution as punishment for Nördlingen’s support of the Protestant Schmalkaldic League (1546–1547); it replaced guild-based government with a council of fifteen magistrates appointed by co-optation for life.↩︎

  2. Although Equation 2 is written as a TWFE specification, it defines the estimand (ATT) rather than the regression actually run: the paper estimates the ATT with the de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) estimator, which targets it via clean \(2\times 2\) comparisons (each newly-treated taxpayer against the not-yet-treated cohort) rather than OLS.↩︎

  3. The published equation (3) is notationally ambiguous: it reuses the calendar-time index \(t\) as the summation index (clashing with \(\pi_t\)) and carries a single \(\beta\) outside the sum, although the paper plots one coefficient per period and refers to “the betas” (p. 537). The printed range \(-2,\ldots,7\) does not match the replication code: did_multiplegt is called with placebo(3) dynamic(5), yielding 3 placebos and 5 dynamic effects. Figure 3 trims visually to \(k=-3,-2\); I retain all 3 placebos in Figure 1 to inform the sensitivity analysis in Section 5.↩︎

  4. Three of the six event-study panels of Figure 3 and the “+ Controls” panels of Figures 4–6 require more memory than a 16 GB machine permits, owing to the 60-dimensional occupational control set combined with 100-replication clustered bootstrap. The estimation calls are included in replication.R but their outputs are not.↩︎

  5. The “+ Controls” panels of Figure 3 (Panels A.II, B.II, C.II) are computationally demanding: the 60 occupational dummies combined with 100-replication bootstrap exceed the memory available on a 16 GB machine. The estimation code is included in replication.R. The figure also retains all three placebos returned by the placebo(3) option in Schaff (2024)’s did_multiplegt call, whereas the published figure trims visually to two via trimlead(2); this allows the Rambachan and Roth (2023) sensitivity analysis in Section 5 to use the full set of pre-period coefficients.↩︎

  6. The author treats the clerk treatment as artificially absorbing to keep DCDH’s “switcher” comparisons clean (Schaff (2024), footnote 12). This redefines the estimand: the ATT for clerks captures the cumulative effect of having served, not the instantaneous effect of currently serving.↩︎

  7. The differences relevant to Nördlingen are technical: Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) builds cohort-specific ATTs using long differences against the never-treated, whereas DCDH uses first differences with not-yet-treated comparisons. With Nördlingen’s small cohorts (typically one to three new magistrates per year), cohort-specific estimates under Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) would carry substantial sampling variance, making a direct horse-race uninformative.↩︎

  8. Rambachan and Roth (2023) is designed for event-studies estimated by OLS/TWFE. The bootstrap-based vcov produced by did_multiplegt_dyn is approximately diagonal and is not suitable input. I therefore estimate the event-study via two-way fixed effects with fixest::feols() and apply the sensitivity analysis to that estimate — the same TWFE specification Schaff (2024) reports in his Online Appendix 5.↩︎

  9. Two technical limitations: (i) the TWFE event-study point estimate (~0.29 at \(k=0\)) differs from the DCDH ATT (0.526) because TWFE under heterogeneous effects targets a weighted combination of \(2\times 2\) comparisons rather than a pure ATT (Goodman-Bacon 2021). The sensitivity profile applies to the TWFE estimand, but the substantive lesson generalises since DCDH shares the same parallel-trends assumption. (ii) The relative-magnitudes restriction is one of several available in Rambachan and Roth (2023); a smoothness restriction would yield somewhat different breakdown values.↩︎
